questions.sec: AKI definition & KDIGO classification · p796
questions.q: Acute kidney injury is defined as an abrupt decrease in renal function over hours to days resulting in:
opts: ECF volume expansion, uremia, hyperkalemia and acidosis
ECF volume depletion with hyponatremia and alkalosis
questions.exp: AKI: abrupt decrease in renal function over hours to days resulting in (a) ECF volume expansion, (b) uremia, (c) hyperkalemia and (d) acidosis. (Book p796)

questions.sec: AKI definition & KDIGO classification · p796
questions.q: Fill up: The four consequences of AKI listed are ECF volume expansion, uremia, hyperkalemia and ______.
questions.exp: AKI results in ECF volume expansion, uremia, hyperkalemia and acidosis. (Book p796)

questions.sec: AKI definition & KDIGO classification · p796
questions.q: Match the KDIGO stage with its urine-output criterion — 1) KDIGO 1  2) KDIGO 2  3) KDIGO 3 … A) <0.3 mL/kg/hr for ≥24 hrs or anuria (≤100 mL) for ≥12 hrs  B) <0.5 mL/kg/hr for ≥6 hrs  C) <0.5 mL/kg/hr for ≥12 hrs
questions.exp: KDIGO urine-output criteria: stage 1 — <0.5 mL/kg/hr for ≥6 hrs; stage 2 — <0.5 mL/kg/hr for ≥12 hrs; stage 3 — <0.3 mL/kg/hr for ≥24 hrs or anuria (≤100 mL) for ≥12 hrs. (Book p796)

questions.sec: AKI definition & KDIGO classification · p796
questions.q: KDIGO stage 1 is met by a urine output of less than 0.5 mL/kg/hr for at least:
questions.exp: KDIGO 1: urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for ≥6 hrs. (Book p796)

questions.sec: AKI definition & KDIGO classification · p796
questions.q: Match the KDIGO stage with its creatinine criterion — 1) KDIGO 1  2) KDIGO 2  3) KDIGO 3 … A) Raised by >3 times the baseline  B) Raised by >0.3 mg/dL or >50% in 7 days (1.5–1.9 times baseline)  C) Raised by >2 times the baseline
questions.exp: KDIGO creatinine criteria: stage 1 — rise >0.3 mg/dL or >50% in 7 days (1.5–1.9 times baseline); stage 2 — >2 times baseline; stage 3 — >3 times baseline. (Book p796)

questions.sec: AKI definition & KDIGO classification · p796
questions.q: A patient's creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.3 mg/dL over 3 days with urine output of 0.4 mL/kg/hr for 14 hours. The KDIGO stage is:
opts: KDIGO 2 — creatinine >2 times baseline and urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for ≥12 hrs
Not AKI — the creatinine rise is physiological
questions.exp: Creatinine >2 times baseline (stage 2 creatinine) with urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for ≥12 hrs (stage 2 urine criterion) = KDIGO 2. (Book p796)

questions.sec: AKI definition & KDIGO classification · p796
questions.q: A man with creatinine 1.2 mg/dL develops anuria with 90 mL of urine over the last 14 hours. KDIGO stage is:
opts: AKI cannot be staged without a creatinine rise
questions.exp: KDIGO 3 urine criterion: <0.3 mL/kg/hr for ≥24 hrs OR anuria (≤100 mL) for ≥12 hrs. (Book p796)

questions.sec: AKI definition & KDIGO classification · p796
questions.q: Which set lists only the newer markers of AKI given in the note?
opts: NGAL, KIM-1, cystatin C and β₂ microglobulin
KIM-1, IL-18, troponin and brain natriuretic peptide
LFABP, IL-18, C-reactive protein and procalcitonin
questions.exp: Note: the newer markers in AKI are NGAL, KIM-1, LFABP and IL-18. (Book p796)

questions.sec: AKI definition & KDIGO classification · p796
questions.q: All but one of the following are listed as newer markers of AKI. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Newer AKI markers listed: NGAL, KIM-1, LFABP and IL-18. (Book p796)

questions.sec: AKI definition & KDIGO classification · p796
questions.q: In the CAUSES flowchart, the renal causes of AKI are:
opts: Acute tubular necrosis and acute interstitial nephritis
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and HUS only
questions.exp: The CAUSES flowchart divides AKI into pre-renal, renal and post-renal; the renal branch names acute tubular necrosis (ATN) and acute interstitial nephritis (AIN). (Book p796)

questions.sec: Pre-renal AKI causes · p796
questions.q: Pre-renal AKI is labelled as:
opts: The commonest cause of hospital AKI
The rarest cause of hospital AKI
questions.exp: Pre-renal AKI is marked as the commonest cause of hospital AKI, with the causes grouped from intravascular volume depletion to compartment syndrome. (Book p796)

questions.sec: Pre-renal AKI causes · p796
questions.q: Match each pre-renal cause with its category — 1) Hemorrhage/blood loss  2) Cirrhosis  3) Cardiorenal syndrome  4) Sepsis … A) Widespread systemic vasodilation  B) ↓Cardiac output  C) Intravascular volume depletion  D) Reduced effective intravascular volume
questions.exp: Pre-renal causes: intravascular volume depletion (haemorrhage, upper GI bleeding, vomiting/diarrhoea, NG loss, diuretic overuse, diabetes insipidus); reduced effective intravascular volume (cirrhosis, cardiac failure, hypoalbuminemia/nephrotic syndrome, third-space sequestration); ↓cardiac output (cardiorenal syndrome); systemic vasodilation (sepsis). (Book p796)

questions.sec: Pre-renal AKI causes · p796
questions.q: All but one of the following are causes of intravascular volume depletion in pre-renal AKI. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Cirrhosis acts through reduced effective intravascular volume (splanchnic vasodilation), not true volume depletion, which is caused by haemorrhage, GI losses, diuretics and diabetes insipidus. (Book p796)

questions.sec: Pre-renal AKI causes · p796
questions.q: A patient with cirrhosis has a rising creatinine. The proposed mechanism in the list of pre-renal causes is:
opts: Reduced effective intravascular volume due to splanchnic vasodilation
Acute tubular necrosis from bile pigments
True intravascular volume depletion from haemorrhage
questions.exp: Pre-renal AKI group 2: reduced effective intravascular volume — cirrhosis (due to splanchnic vasodilation), cardiac failure and hypoalbuminemia/nephrotic syndrome. (Book p796)

questions.sec: Pre-renal AKI causes · p796
questions.q: Match the third-space sequestration causes — 1) Burns  2) Rhabdomyolysis  3) Acute pancreatitis … A) All are grouped as third-space sequestration
opts: All three are grouped as third-space sequestration
None of them is a pre-renal cause
questions.exp: Third-space sequestration (under reduced effective intravascular volume): burns, rhabdomyolysis and acute pancreatitis. (Book p796)

questions.sec: Pre-renal AKI causes · p796
questions.q: A patient with acute pancreatitis develops oliguric AKI. Which group of pre-renal causes covers this?
questions.exp: Burns, rhabdomyolysis and acute pancreatitis are grouped under third-space sequestration, a component of reduced effective intravascular volume. (Book p796)

questions.sec: Pre-renal AKI causes · p796
questions.q: Match the renal vasoconstriction causes — 1) Hepatorenal syndrome  2) Hypercalcemia  3) Drugs … A) NSAIDs, calcineurin inhibitors, ACEi/ARBs  B) Hepatorenal syndrome  C) Hypercalcemia
questions.exp: Renal vasoconstriction (pre-renal cause 5): hepatorenal syndrome, hypercalcemia and drugs — NSAIDs, calcineurin inhibitors and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. (Book p796)

questions.sec: Pre-renal AKI causes · p796
questions.q: Fill up: Among the drugs causing pre-renal AKI by renal vasoconstriction, the book lists NSAIDs, calcineurin inhibitors and ______/ARBs.
questions.exp: Renal vasoconstriction drugs: NSAIDs, calcineurin inhibitors and ACEi/ARBs — all impair renal autoregulation. (Book p796)

questions.sec: Pre-renal AKI causes · p796
questions.q: Sepsis produces pre-renal AKI by widespread systemic vasodilation.
questions.exp: Pre-renal cause 4: widespread systemic vasodilation — sepsis. (Book p796)

questions.sec: Pre-renal AKI causes · p796
questions.q: All but one of the following are listed pre-renal causes of AKI. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Pre-renal causes listed include diabetes insipidus, cardiorenal syndrome and compartment syndrome (cause 6). Renal lymphoma is a renal (AIN by infiltration) cause. (Book p796)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: Match the three conditions bracketed together as 'pre-renal >> ATN' in drug/insult-induced AKI — 1) NSAIDs  2) Rhabdomyolysis  3) Polyuria (contrast-induced AKI) … A) Pre-renal component predominates over ATN
opts: All three have a pre-renal component predominant over ATN
None of them has a pre-renal component
questions.exp: NSAIDs, rhabdomyolysis and polyuria (contrast-induced AKI) are bracketed together as 'pre-renal >> ATN', i.e. the pre-renal component predominates. (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: Which is the commonest form of pre-renal failure described in the pathophysiology section?
questions.exp: Pathophysiology 1: non-oliguric failure (m/c). Oliguric pre-renal failure occurs only with renal vasoconstriction (NSAIDs/hypercalcemia/HRS). (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: Oliguric pre-renal failure occurs only with renal vasoconstriction, as with NSAIDs, hypercalcemia or hepatorenal syndrome.
opts: False — oliguric pre-renal failure occurs with any volume depletion
False — oliguric failure is the rule in all pre-renal AKI
questions.exp: Oliguric pre-renal failure occurs only with renal vasoconstriction (NSAIDs/hypercalcemia/HRS); otherwise pre-renal failure is non-oliguric. (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: Complete the flowchart of long-standing profound pre-renal failure — 1) Resulting tubular lesion  2) Feedback mechanism  3) Consequences … A) Tubuloglomerular feedback by macula densa → ↓GFR → ↓urine output  B) Ischemic ATN
questions.exp: Flowchart: long-standing profound pre-renal failure → ischemic ATN → tubuloglomerular feedback by macula densa → ↓GFR → ↓urine output. (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: Fill up: In ischemic ATN, tubuloglomerular feedback is mediated by the ______.
questions.exp: Tubuloglomerular feedback by the macula densa causes ↓GFR and ↓urine output in ischemic ATN. (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: The two broad mechanisms of ATN are:
opts: Immune complex deposition and complement activation
questions.exp: Renal AKI — ATN: ischemia and toxins (the toxins being endogenous and exogenous). (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: Match each endogenous toxin with its source — 1) Hemoglobin  2) Myoglobin  3) Uric acid  4) Light chains … A) Multiple myeloma  B) Hemolysis  C) Rhabdomyolysis  D) Uric acid nephropathy
questions.exp: Endogenous toxins causing ATN: hemoglobin (hemolysis), myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis), uric acid (uric acid nephropathy) and light chains (multiple myeloma). (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: A patient in a crush injury develops AKI with pigmented urine. Which endogenous toxin is responsible?
questions.exp: Endogenous toxin list: hemoglobin (hemolysis), myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis), uric acid (uric acid nephropathy) and light chains (multiple myeloma). (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: Fill up: In ATN, the two listed exogenous toxins are drugs and ______.
questions.exp: Exogenous toxins in ATN: drugs and contrast. (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: The ATN histology figure is labelled with flattened epithelium and intraluminal debris. These changes correspond to:
opts: Tubular injury of acute tubular necrosis
Interstitial infiltrate of acute interstitial nephritis
questions.exp: The ATN figure labels flattened epithelium and intraluminal debris, the histological correlates of tubular injury in ATN. (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is caused by:
opts: Hypersensitivity reactions — drugs, infections and infiltration
Ischemic injury of the proximal tubule alone, without any immune mechanism
Contrast media alone, acting through medullary hypoxia and tubular injury
Cholesterol embolization of small renal vessels from an aortic plaque
questions.exp: AIN (hypersensitivity reactions): drugs; infections — leptospirosis and scrub typhus; infiltration — lymphoma and sarcoidosis. (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: Match the AIN subgroups — 1) Infections  2) Infiltration … A) Lymphoma and sarcoidosis  B) Leptospirosis and scrub typhus
questions.exp: AIN causes: drugs; infections — leptospirosis, scrub typhus; infiltration — lymphoma, sarcoidosis. (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: All but one of the following are listed causes of acute interstitial nephritis. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Leptospirosis/scrub typhus (infections) and lymphoma (infiltration) cause AIN; ethylene glycol is an ATN toxin producing oxalate urine crystals. (Book p797)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN exceptions & pathophysiology · p797
questions.q: Rhabdomyolysis is listed both as a pre-renal cause (third-space sequestration) and as a cause of ATN through myoglobin.
opts: True — it appears in both lists
False — it causes only pre-renal AKI
True, but only when urine pH is alkaline
questions.exp: Rhabdomyolysis appears under third-space sequestration (pre-renal) and as an endogenous ATN toxin (myoglobin), explaining why 'pre-renal >> ATN' is bracketed for it. (Book p797)

questions.sec: Drugs causing AKI: four-column classification · p798
questions.q: Match each drug class with its column in the drug-induced AKI chart — 1) NSAIDs  2) Vancomycin and aminoglycosides  3) Methotrexate and indinavir  4) PPIs and beta-lactams … A) AIN  B) Pre-renal failure  C) ATN  D) Intratubular obstruction (oliguric AKI)
questions.exp: Drug chart: pre-renal failure — NSAIDs, drugs causing ↑Ca²⁺, ACEi/ARB, calcineurin inhibitors; ATN — vancomycin, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, cisplatin, ethylene glycol, salicylates; intratubular obstruction (oliguric AKI) — methotrexate (increased dose), indinavir, triamterene, acyclovir, sulfonamides; AIN — PPIs, beta-lactams, rifampicin, allopurinol and anticonvulsants (also NSAIDs and diuretics). (Book p798)

questions.sec: Drugs causing AKI: four-column classification · p798
questions.q: All but one of the following drugs cause ATN. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Triamterene is grouped under intratubular obstruction (oliguric AKI) along with methotrexate, indinavir, acyclovir and sulfonamides; vancomycin, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B and cisplatin belong to ATN. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Drugs causing AKI: four-column classification · p798
questions.q: Match the mnemonic letters in the ATN column — 1) V  2) A  3) C  4) E … A) Ethylene glycol (oxalate urine crystals)  B) Vancomycin  C) Aminoglycosides, adefovir, amphotericin B  D) Cisplatin, cyclophosphamide, cidofovir
questions.exp: ATN mnemonic: V — vancomycin; A — aminoglycosides, adefovir, amphotericin B; C — cisplatin, cyclophosphamide, cidofovir; E — ethylene glycol (oxalate urine crystals); S — salicylates. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Drugs causing AKI: four-column classification · p798
questions.q: A patient with ethylene glycol poisoning has oxalate crystals in the urine. In the drug chart, ethylene glycol is classified under:
questions.exp: Ethylene glycol is listed in the ATN column with the annotation 'oxalate urine crystals'. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Drugs causing AKI: four-column classification · p798
questions.q: Match the mnemonic letters in the intratubular obstruction column — 1) m  2) I  3) T  4) A  5) S … A) Methotrexate (increased dose)  B) Indinavir  C) Triamterene  D) Acyclovir  E) Sulfonamides
questions.exp: Intratubular obstruction (oliguric AKI) mnemonic: m — methotrexate (increased dose); I — indinavir; T — triamterene; A — acyclovir; S — sulfonamides. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Drugs causing AKI: four-column classification · p798
questions.q: Match the AIN column drugs — 1) PPIs  2) β lactams  3) Rifampicin  4) Allopurinol and anticonvulsants  5) NSAIDs and diuretics … A) All appear in the AIN column
opts: All are listed in the AIN column
Only PPIs and beta-lactams are in the AIN column
Only allopurinol is in the AIN column
None is in the AIN column
questions.exp: AIN column: PPIs; β lactams; rifampicin; allopurinol, anticonvulsants; and NSAIDs, diuretics — remembered by the mnemonic. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Drugs causing AKI: four-column classification · p798
questions.q: A patient started on indinavir for HIV develops oliguric AKI. The mechanism in the drug chart is:
questions.exp: Indinavir is listed in the intratubular obstruction column, which is described as oliguric AKI. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Drugs causing AKI: four-column classification · p798
questions.q: NSAIDs appear in the drug chart both as a pre-renal cause and in the AIN column.
opts: False — NSAIDs appear only as a pre-renal cause
False — NSAIDs appear only under ATN
questions.exp: NSAIDs are listed under pre-renal failure and again in the AIN column (with diuretics), reflecting their dual mechanisms. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Drugs causing AKI: four-column classification · p798
questions.q: All but one of the following drugs cause intratubular obstruction. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Adefovir is in the ATN column (with aminoglycosides and amphotericin B); methotrexate, acyclovir, sulfonamides and triamterene cause intratubular obstruction. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Drugs causing AKI: four-column classification · p798
questions.q: Which drug group is listed under pre-renal failure as causing ↑serum calcium in the drug chart?
questions.exp: Pre-renal failure column: NSAIDs; drugs causing ↑Ca²⁺ (hypercalcemia); ACEi/ARB; calcineurin inhibitors. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: Match the urine output and albumin in the pre-renal vs ATN table — 1) Pre-renal AKI urine output  2) Pre-renal urine albumin  3) ATN urine albumin … A) ↓  B) Normal  C) 1+  D) (–) absent
questions.exp: Table: pre-renal — urine output normal, urine albumin absent (–); ATN — urine output ↓, urine albumin 1+. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: Urine microscopy shows muddy brown epithelial casts. According to the table this finding belongs to:
questions.exp: Table: urine microscopy is (–) in pre-renal AKI and shows muddy brown epithelial casts in ATN. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: The BUN/creatinine ratio in pre-renal AKI is:
questions.exp: Table: BUN/creatinine ratio >20 in pre-renal AKI and <10 in ATN. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: In the pre-renal vs ATN table, the urine sodium in ATN is:
questions.exp: Table: urine Na⁺ <20 mEq/L in pre-renal AKI and >40 mEq/L in ATN. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: Match urine creatinine and FeNa in the table — 1) Pre-renal urine creatinine  2) ATN urine creatinine  3) Pre-renal FeNa  4) ATN FeNa … A) >40  B) <20  C) <1%  D) >2%
questions.exp: Table: urine creatinine >40 (pre-renal) versus <20 (ATN); FeNa <1% (pre-renal) versus >2% (ATN) — FeNa being marked as the best parameter. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: The table marks FeNa as the best discriminator between pre-renal AKI and ATN.
opts: False — urine sodium is marked as best
False — the BUN/creatinine ratio is marked as best
False — no single parameter is marked
questions.exp: In the table, FeNa carries the annotation '(Best)' — urine osmolality and specific gravity are normal in pre-renal AKI and ↓ in ATN, while urine pH is normal in pre-renal and rises in ATN. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: Match urine osmolality, specific gravity and pH — 1) Pre-renal urine osmolality  2) ATN urine specific gravity  3) ATN urine pH … A) Normal  B) ↓  C) ↑
questions.exp: Table: pre-renal — urine osmolality normal, specific gravity normal, pH normal; ATN — osmolality ↓, specific gravity ↓, pH ↑. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: The treatment row of the pre-renal versus ATN table is:
opts: Fluids for pre-renal AKI and treatment of the cause for ATN
Dialysis for pre-renal AKI and fluids for ATN
Steroids for pre-renal AKI and diuretics for ATN
questions.exp: Rx row: fluids for pre-renal AKI; Rx of cause for ATN. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: Fill up: The formula for fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) is (u.Na/u.Creatinine) × (______/S.Na).
questions.exp: FeNa = (u. Na / u. Creatinine) × (S. Creatinine / S. Na); normal is 1–2%. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: The normal value of FeNa is:
questions.exp: Normal FeNa: 1–2%. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: Why is FeNa reduced in pre-renal failure?
opts: Sodium reabsorption is increased (↓ urine Na) and creatinine secretion is increased (↑ urine creatinine)
Sodium reabsorption falls (↑ urine Na), while urine creatinine also falls
Both urine Na and urine creatinine fall, so the calculated ratio is unchanged
Aldosterone secretion is suppressed, so both urine Na and creatinine rise
questions.exp: ↓FeNa in pre-renal failure occurs because Na⁺ reabsorption is increased (↓u.Na) and creatinine secretion is increased (↑u.Creatinine). (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: Match the three ATN conditions with FeNa <1% — 1) NSAIDs  2) Rhabdomyolysis  3) Contrast AKI … A) All three can show FeNa <1% because the pre-renal component predominates
opts: All three are listed as ATN with FeNa <1%
Only contrast AKI can show FeNa <1%
None of them can show FeNa <1%
questions.exp: ATN with FeNa <1%: NSAIDs, rhabdomyolysis and contrast AKI — the pre-renal component is predominant in these. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Pre-renal vs ATN table & FeNa · p798
questions.q: All but one of the following favour ATN over pre-renal AKI. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Urine Na⁺ <20 mEq/L favours pre-renal AKI; muddy brown casts, BUN/creatinine <10 and FeNa >2% all favour ATN. (Book p798)

questions.sec: Acute interstitial nephritis · p799
questions.q: Acute interstitial nephritis is:
opts: A hypersensitivity reaction (T₄ mediated) causing reversible AKI
An ischemic injury of the proximal tubule
questions.exp: AIN: hypersensitivity reaction (T₄ mediated), causing reversible AKI. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Acute interstitial nephritis · p799
questions.q: Fill up: AIN is a ______ reaction, T₄ mediated, causing reversible AKI.
questions.exp: AIN is a hypersensitivity reaction that is T₄ mediated and produces reversible AKI. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Acute interstitial nephritis · p799
questions.q: Match the AIN clinical features — 1) Rash, eosinophilia  2) Renal failure  3) Edema and hypertension  4) Flank pain, haematuria, pyuria … A) Asymptomatic  B) Absent  C) Rare  D) Present with eosinophilia
questions.exp: AIN clinical features: rash and eosinophilia; renal failure may be asymptomatic; no edema or HTN; flank pain, haematuria and pyuria are rare. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Acute interstitial nephritis · p799
questions.q: Edema and hypertension are characteristically absent in acute interstitial nephritis.
opts: True — AIN presents with neither oedema nor HTN
False — oedema is the rule in AIN
False — hypertension is the earliest sign of AIN
questions.exp: AIN clinical features: no edema, no HTN (in contrast with glomerular and volume-overload AKI). (Book p799)

questions.sec: Acute interstitial nephritis · p799
questions.q: A patient started on an antibiotic 10 days ago now has a maculopapular rash, eosinophilia and a rising creatinine with no oedema or hypertension. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.exp: AIN: hypersensitivity reaction with rash and eosinophilia, asymptomatic renal failure without oedema/HTN (maculopapular rash figure). (Book p799)

questions.sec: Acute interstitial nephritis · p799
questions.q: Match the AIN investigations — 1) RFT  2) Urinalysis  3) Renal biopsy … A) Interstitial infiltrates with a normal glomerulus  B) Impaired  C) Mild proteinuria with occasional WBC casts
questions.exp: AIN investigations: impaired RFT; urinalysis — mild proteinuria with occasional WBC casts; renal biopsy — interstitial infiltrates with a normal glomerulus. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Acute interstitial nephritis · p799
questions.q: The renal biopsy finding in acute interstitial nephritis is:
opts: Interstitial infiltrates with a normal glomerulus
Crescentic proliferation of parietal epithelial cells
questions.exp: Renal biopsy in AIN: interstitial infiltrates + normal glomerulus. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Acute interstitial nephritis · p799
questions.q: Fill up: The urinalysis in AIN shows mild proteinuria and occasional ______ casts.
questions.exp: Urinalysis in AIN: mild proteinuria with occasional WBC casts (not RBC or muddy brown casts). (Book p799)

questions.sec: Acute interstitial nephritis · p799
questions.q: The treatment of acute interstitial nephritis consists of:
opts: Stop the insult, then steroids (the mainstay) after 1 week
Continue the drug with high-dose diuretics
questions.exp: Treatment of AIN: stop the insult; after 1 week, steroids (mainstay). (Book p799)

questions.sec: Acute interstitial nephritis · p799
questions.q: In the treatment of AIN, steroids are started after:
questions.exp: AIN treatment: stop the insult, and after 1 week steroids are the mainstay — the delay allows spontaneous recovery from the hypersensitivity. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Acute interstitial nephritis · p799
questions.q: All but one of the following are features of AIN. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Interstitial infiltrates with normal glomeruli on biopsy
questions.exp: AIN is characterised by the absence of oedema and HTN; rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts and interstitial infiltrates with normal glomeruli all belong to AIN. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Drug-induced nephropathy: NSAIDs and aminoglycosides · p799
questions.q: Complete the NSAID pathophysiology flowchart — 1) NSAIDs act on PGE₂/PGI₂  2) Effect on RAAS  3) Final step … A) ↑K⁺ excretion via aldosterone  B) (–) inhibition  C) Stimulation of RAAS
questions.exp: NSAID flowchart: NSAIDs (–) PGE₂/PGI₂ → stimulates RAAS → aldosterone → ↑K⁺ excretion. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Drug-induced nephropathy: NSAIDs and aminoglycosides · p799
questions.q: A 60-year-old on long-term NSAIDs develops AKI with a urine output of 400 mL/day, FeNa of 0.7% and a K⁺ of 6.4 mEq/L. Which statement matches the book's description?
opts: Oliguria, FeNa <1 and hyperkalemia out of proportion to the renal failure
Polyuria, FeNa <1 and hypokalemia out of proportion to the renal failure
Oliguria, FeNa >2 and hypokalemia with an active urinary sediment
Anuria, FeNa >2 and hyperkalemia with muddy brown epithelial casts
questions.exp: NSAID nephropathy clinical features: oliguria, FeNa <1 and hyperkalemia out of proportion. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Drug-induced nephropathy: NSAIDs and aminoglycosides · p799
questions.q: All but one of the following are features of NSAID-induced nephropathy. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: NSAID nephropathy: oliguria, FeNa <1 and hyperkalemia out of proportion; FeNa >2% indicates established ATN. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Drug-induced nephropathy: NSAIDs and aminoglycosides · p799
questions.q: Complete the aminoglycoside pathophysiology flowchart — 1) Cationic amino groups on the drug  2) Target  3) Intracellular effect … A) Binds anionic megalin in the brush border of the PCT  B) Accumulates in lysosomes after endocytosis causing oxidative stress  C) Anionic megalin

questions.sec: Drug-induced nephropathy: NSAIDs and aminoglycosides · p799
questions.q: Aminoglycosides are taken up into proximal tubular cells by binding to:

questions.exp: Cationic amino groups on aminoglycosides bind anionic megalin in the brush border of the PCT, are endocytosed, and accumulate in lysosomes causing oxidative stress. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Drug-induced nephropathy: NSAIDs and aminoglycosides · p799
questions.q: A patient given gentamicin develops non-oliguric AKI on day 7 of therapy. Which drug-related pattern is described?
opts: Non-oliguric AKI 5–10 days after starting the drug

questions.sec: Drug-induced nephropathy: NSAIDs and aminoglycosides · p799
questions.q: How is aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity prevented according to the page?

Give smaller divided doses three times a day
Combine with a loop diuretic to increase excretion
Give with NSAIDs to reduce tubular inflammation

questions.sec: Drug-induced nephropathy: NSAIDs and aminoglycosides · p799
questions.q: Aminoglycoside-induced non-oliguric AKI typically appears how long after the drug?
questions.exp: Aminoglycoside clinical features: non-oliguric AKI 5–10 days after the drug. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Drug-induced nephropathy: NSAIDs and aminoglycosides · p799
questions.q: All but one of the following are correct about aminoglycoside nephropathy. Which is the odd one out?
opts: It binds megalin in the PCT brush border
It accumulates in lysosomes causing oxidative stress
It appears 5–10 days after the drug
questions.exp: Aminoglycosides cause non-oliguric AKI (5–10 days after the drug), with the megalin-lysosome-oxidative stress mechanism. (Book p799)

questions.sec: Drug-induced nephropathy: NSAIDs and aminoglycosides · p799
questions.q: Both NSAID and aminoglycoside nephropathy involve active reabsorption pathways in the proximal nephron.
opts: False — only aminoglycosides are taken up by megalin-mediated endocytosis in the PCT
True — NSAIDs are also taken up by megalin-mediated endocytosis in the PCT
False — aminoglycosides act only on the collecting duct, not on the proximal tubule
True, but only when NSAIDs are given together with an aminoglycoside drug
questions.exp: Aminoglycosides are endocytosed after binding anionic megalin in the PCT brush border; NSAIDs act by inhibiting PGE₂/PGI₂, stimulating RAAS. (Book p799)

questions.sec: ATN phases and the hypercalcemia/hypernatremia note · p800
questions.q: Match the three phases of ATN described — 1) Phase 1 tubular injury  2) Phase 2 tubuloglomerular feedback  3) Phase 3 … A) ↓GFR from adenosine-mediated afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction  B) Loss of solutes and water  C) Recovery
questions.exp: ATN phases: 1 — tubular injury with loss of solutes and water; 2 — tubuloglomerular feedback → ↓GFR; 3 — recovery. (Book p800)

questions.sec: ATN phases and the hypercalcemia/hypernatremia note · p800
questions.q: In ATN, the fall in urine output is mediated by:
questions.exp: ATN phase 2: ↓urine output from adenosine-mediated afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, with ↑S. phosphorus, ↓S. Ca²⁺, ↑mg²⁺ and hyponatremia all reducing GFR. (Book p800)

questions.sec: ATN phases and the hypercalcemia/hypernatremia note · p800
questions.q: Match each ATN electrolyte acid-base change — 1) Serum phosphorus  2) Serum calcium  3) Serum magnesium  4) Serum sodium … A) ↓  B) ↑  C) ↑  D) ↓ (hyponatremia)
questions.exp: ATN phase 2: ↑S. phosphorus, ↓S. Ca²⁺, ↑mg²⁺ and hyponatremia, all grouped with the fall in GFR. (Book p800)

questions.sec: ATN phases and the hypercalcemia/hypernatremia note · p800
questions.q: Match the complications of ATN — 1) Uremia  2) Volume overload  3) Acidosis  4) Potassium … A) ↑K⁺  B) NAGMA  C) Present  D) Present
questions.exp: ATN complications: uremia, volume overload, acidosis (NAGMA — normal anion gap metabolic acidosis) and ↑K⁺. (Book p800)

questions.sec: ATN phases and the hypercalcemia/hypernatremia note · p800
questions.q: Fill up: The acidosis of ATN is described as ______.
questions.exp: ATN complications include acidosis (NAGMA) and ↑K⁺ along with uremia and volume overload. (Book p800)

questions.sec: ATN phases and the hypercalcemia/hypernatremia note · p800
questions.q: Hypercalcemia and hypernatremia are not seen in AKI.
opts: False — both are typical of AKI
False — hypercalcemia is typical but hypernatremia is not
True, but only for stage 3 AKI
questions.exp: Note: hypercalcemia and hypernatremia are not seen in AKI (indeed calcium falls and hyponatremia occurs), whereas hyperkalaemia and acidosis are characteristic. (Book p800)

questions.sec: ATN phases and the hypercalcemia/hypernatremia note · p800
questions.q: A patient with ATN is in the recovery phase. Which phase number and description apply?
opts: Phase 1 — tubular injury with loss of solutes and water
There is no recovery phase in ATN
questions.exp: ATN phases are 1 — tubular injury, 2 — tubuloglomerular feedback with ↓GFR, 3 — recovery. (Book p800)

questions.sec: ATN phases and the hypercalcemia/hypernatremia note · p800
questions.q: All but one of the following biochemical changes are seen in ATN. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: In ATN, S. Ca²⁺ falls (↓); phosphorus, magnesium and uric acid rise with hyponatremia. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis: pathophysiology, causes and clinical features · p800
questions.q: Complete the sepsis pathophysiology flowchart — 1) Pre-renal component  2) Macrovascular change  3) Microvascular change … A) Widespread systemic vasodilation  B) Microthrombi + endothelial leak  C) Predominant over ATN
questions.exp: Sepsis flowchart: pre-renal (predominant) >> ATN; widespread systemic vasodilation (macrovascular) + microthrombi + endothelial leak (microvascular) → ↓↓ kidney perfusion. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis: pathophysiology, causes and clinical features · p800
questions.q: In sepsis, the pre-renal component predominates over ATN, and microthrombi with endothelial leak cause ↓↓ kidney perfusion.
opts: False — ATN predominates from the outset
False — there is no pre-renal component in sepsis
True, but only in fungal sepsis
questions.exp: Sepsis flowchart: pre-renal (predominant) >> ATN, with vasodilation plus microthrombi and endothelial leak reducing kidney perfusion. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis: pathophysiology, causes and clinical features · p800
questions.q: Match the sepsis ATN pathway — 1) ↑PAMPs, DAMPs  2) Next step  3) Result … A) Inflammatory cascade  B) Oxidative stress  C) Released in ATN
questions.exp: ATN arm of the sepsis flowchart: ↑PAMPs, DAMPs → inflammatory cascade → oxidative stress. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis: pathophysiology, causes and clinical features · p800
questions.q: Match the causes of sepsis-associated AKI — 1) Urosepsis  2) CRBSI  3) Diabetic nephropathy with soft tissue infection (cellulitis) … A) Cellulitis  B) Urosepsis  C) Catheter related bloodstream infection
questions.exp: Causes of sepsis in this section: urosepsis; CRBSI (catheter related blood stream infection); DM nephropathy with soft tissue infection (cellulitis); also renal allograft recipients, UTI and post-operative patients. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis: pathophysiology, causes and clinical features · p800
questions.q: The sepsis causes listed besides urosepsis, CRBSI and cellulitis are:
opts: Renal allograft recipients, UTI and post-operative state
Cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome and heart failure
questions.exp: Causes list: urosepsis, CRBSI, DM nephropathy with soft tissue infection (cellulitis), renal allograft recipients, UTI and post-operative. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis: pathophysiology, causes and clinical features · p800
questions.q: In early sepsis, why may the skin feel warm despite poor end-organ perfusion?
opts: Because blood flow is redirected, so the skin is warm in the early phase (cool skin later)
Because the patient is febrile from the infection only
questions.exp: Signs of poor end-organ perfusion: HR >90/min, cool skin (redirection of blood flow) — warm in the early phase — with ↓urine output and restlessness. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis: pathophysiology, causes and clinical features · p800
questions.q: Match each sign of poor end-organ perfusion in sepsis — 1) Heart rate  2) Skin  3) Urine output  4) Sensorium … A) Restlessness  B) >90/min  C) Cool skin (warm early)  D) ↓
questions.exp: Sepsis clinical features (signs of poor end-organ perfusion): HR >90/min; cool skin (redirection of blood flow), warm in the early phase; ↓urine output; restlessness. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis: pathophysiology, causes and clinical features · p800
questions.q: The heart-rate threshold given among the signs of poor end-organ perfusion in sepsis is:
questions.exp: Signs of poor end-organ perfusion: HR >90/min, plus cool skin, ↓urine output and restlessness. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis: pathophysiology, causes and clinical features · p800
questions.q: All but one of the following are listed as causes of sepsis-related AKI. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Listed causes: urosepsis, CRBSI, DM nephropathy with soft tissue infection (cellulitis), renal allograft recipients, UTI and post-operative state. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis management: investigations · p800
questions.q: The normal IVC diameter used to determine the amount of fluid required is:
questions.exp: Investigations in sepsis-AKI: IVC diameter 2–2.5 cm is normal and determines the amount of fluid required. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis management: investigations · p800
questions.q: Match each serum lactate level with its interpretation — 1) >1 mmol/L  2) >4 mmol/L … A) Severe sepsis  B) Organ hypoperfusion
questions.exp: Serum lactate: >1 mmol/L indicates organ hypoperfusion; >4 mmol/L indicates severe sepsis. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis management: investigations · p800
questions.q: A serum lactate above which value indicates severe sepsis?
questions.exp: Serum lactate >4 mmol/L indicates severe sepsis, while >1 mmol/L denotes organ hypoperfusion. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis management: investigations · p800
questions.q: The passive leg raising test (PLR) is described as:
opts: A test for fluid responsiveness — now obsolete
The investigation of choice for volume status
A test for renal perfusion pressure
questions.exp: Passive leg raising test (PLR): a test for fluid responsiveness, marked obsolete in the book, illustrated by the graph with the 30 mL/kg VE fluid challenge. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis management: investigations · p800
questions.q: Match each sepsis investigation with its purpose — 1) IVC diameter  2) S. Lactate  3) Passive leg raising test … A) Test for fluid responsiveness (obsolete)  B) Determines amount of fluid required  C) Assesses organ hypoperfusion/severe sepsis
questions.exp: Sepsis investigations: IVC diameter (normal 2–2.5 cm) determines the amount of fluid required; serum lactate >1 mmol/L = organ hypoperfusion and >4 mmol/L = severe sepsis; PLR tests fluid responsiveness (obsolete). (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis management: investigations · p800
questions.q: A patient in the ICU has a lactate of 5 mmol/L. According to the book this indicates:
questions.exp: Serum lactate >4 mmol/L indicates severe sepsis (levels >1 mmol/L indicate organ hypoperfusion). (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis management: investigations · p800
questions.q: The passive leg raising test as a test of fluid responsiveness is described as obsolete.
opts: False — it is the investigation of choice
False — it is a test of renal perfusion
questions.exp: PLR is a test for fluid responsiveness, described as obsolete, while IVC diameter and serum lactate remain the listed investigations. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis management: investigations · p800
questions.q: All but one of the following are listed among the investigations for sepsis-associated AKI. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: The listed investigations are IVC diameter (2–2.5 cm normal), serum lactate (>1 and >4 mmol/L thresholds) and the passive leg raising test. (Book p800)

questions.sec: Sepsis treatment ladder & the SAFE trial note · p801
questions.q: Match the treatment steps for sepsis-associated AKI — 1) First line  2) Second line  3) Third line  4) Fourth line … A) Dobutamine  B) Crystalloid  C) Cortisol  D) Vasopressor
questions.exp: Treatment ladder for sepsis-AKI: crystalloid (1st line) → vasopressor (2nd line) with norepinephrine > dopamine → dobutamine → cortisol. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Sepsis treatment ladder & the SAFE trial note · p801
questions.q: The first-line treatment for sepsis-associated AKI is:
questions.exp: Treatment: crystalloid (1st line) → vasopressor (2nd line) → dobutamine → cortisol. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Sepsis treatment ladder & the SAFE trial note · p801
questions.q: A patient with septic shock remains hypotensive after adequate crystalloid. According to the ladder, the next agent is:
opts: Norepinephrine, which is preferred over dopamine
Dobutamine, which is preferred over norepinephrine
questions.exp: Second line: vasopressor — norepinephrine > dopamine; then dobutamine; then cortisol. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Sepsis treatment ladder & the SAFE trial note · p801
questions.q: In sepsis-associated AKI, dopamine is preferred over norepinephrine as the vasopressor.
opts: False — the ladder states norepinephrine > dopamine
True — dopamine is preferred for its renal dose effect
True, but only with concomitant dobutamine
False — vasopressors are not used in sepsis at all
questions.exp: The treatment ladder reads: vasopressor (2nd line) — norepinephrine > dopamine. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Sepsis treatment ladder & the SAFE trial note · p801
questions.q: The trial quoted to establish the efficacy of crystalloids and colloids in sepsis is:
opts: SAFE trial — Saline versus Albumin Fluid Evaluation
SAFE trial — Sepsis and Antibiotics For Everyone
SOAP trial — Saline Or Albumin Protocol
ARISE trial — Albumin Resuscitation In Severe Endotoxaemia
questions.exp: Note: efficacy of crystalloids & colloids established by the SAFE trial — Saline versus Albumin Fluid Evaluation. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Sepsis treatment ladder & the SAFE trial note · p801
questions.q: Diuretics are not used in the prevention or treatment of AKI.
opts: False — diuretics are first line in AKI
False — diuretics are used only in prevention
True, but only in pre-renal AKI
questions.exp: Note: diuretics are not used in the prevention or treatment of AKI — they do not improve renal recovery. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Sepsis treatment ladder & the SAFE trial note · p801
questions.q: A resident suggests furosemide to 'convert oliguric AKI to non-oliguric AKI and improve outcome'. The correct response based on the note is:
opts: Diuretics are not used in prevention or treatment of AKI
Diuretics are the first-line treatment in AKI
Diuretics improve renal recovery if given early
Diuretics are indicated in all oliguric patients
questions.exp: Note: diuretics not used in prevention or treatment of AKI. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Sepsis treatment ladder & the SAFE trial note · p801
questions.q: The ultrasound figure labelled IVC on this page is used to assess:
opts: Volume status by measuring the IVC diameter — normal 2–2.5 cm
Renal size to exclude chronic kidney disease
questions.exp: The IVC ultrasound is shown to assess volume status; the normal IVC diameter is 2–2.5 cm and it determines the amount of fluid required. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Sepsis treatment ladder & the SAFE trial note · p801
questions.q: In the passive leg raising figure, fluid is transferred from the legs and abdominal compartments. The stated purpose is:
opts: A test for fluid responsiveness (obsolete), with the VE 30 mL/kg challenge shown on the graph
A manoeuvre to increase renal perfusion permanently
questions.exp: The PLR figure shows transfer of blood from the legs and abdominal compartments, labelled as a test for fluid responsiveness, with the 30 mL/kg VE (volume expansion) graph before and after. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Sepsis treatment ladder & the SAFE trial note · p801
questions.q: All but one of the following appear in the sepsis-AKI treatment ladder. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: The ladder is crystalloid → vasopressor (norepinephrine > dopamine) → dobutamine → cortisol; diuretics are explicitly not used in prevention or treatment of AKI. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy (tumour lysis syndrome) · p801
questions.q: Uric acid nephropathy is also known as:
questions.exp: Uric acid nephropathy AKA tumour lysis syndrome — a renal cause of AKI. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy (tumour lysis syndrome) · p801
questions.q: Uric acid nephropathy occurs in:
opts: Hematological malignancies within a few days of the onset of treatment
Solid tumours several years after chemotherapy
Chronic kidney disease after contrast exposure
questions.exp: Cause: hematological malignancies within a few days of onset of Rx (chemotherapy). (Book p801)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy (tumour lysis syndrome) · p801
questions.q: Complete the pathophysiology flowchart of uric acid nephropathy — 1) Leukemia/lymphoma  2) Tumour cells  3) Effect … A) Rapid multiplication  B) ↑Uric acid filtered by the glomerulus  C) Underlying malignancy
questions.exp: Flowchart: leukemia/lymphoma → rapid multiplication of tumour cells → ↑uric acid filtered by the glomerulus. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy (tumour lysis syndrome) · p801
questions.q: Match the features of uric acid nephropathy — 1) Renal presentation  2) Serum uric acid  3) Other electrolytes  4) Serum calcium … A) ↑  B) Oliguric AKI  C) S.K⁺/S.PO₄³⁻/S.mg²⁺ ↑  D) ↓S.Ca²⁺
questions.exp: Features of uric acid nephropathy: oliguric AKI; S. uric acid ↑↑; S. K⁺/S. PO₄³⁻/S. mg²⁺ ↑; ↓S. Ca²⁺. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy (tumour lysis syndrome) · p801
questions.q: A 24-year-old with Burkitt lymphoma develops oliguric AKI 3 days after starting chemotherapy, with a uric acid of 14 mg/dL, K⁺ 6.2, PO₄³⁻ 7 mg/dL and Ca²⁺ 7.4 mg/dL. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Uric acid nephropathy (TLS): oliguric AKI with ↑↑uric acid, ↑K⁺/PO₄³⁻/mg²⁺ and ↓Ca²⁺, occurring within days of starting treatment of a haematological malignancy. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy (tumour lysis syndrome) · p801
questions.q: Hypocalcemia is a described feature of uric acid nephropathy.

False — calcium is normal in uric acid nephropathy
questions.exp: Features: oliguric AKI, S. uric acid ↑↑, ↑S.K⁺/S.PO₄³⁻/S.mg²⁺ and ↓S.Ca²⁺. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy (tumour lysis syndrome) · p801
questions.q: The serum potassium, phosphate and magnesium changes in uric acid nephropathy are:
opts: Potassium raised with phosphate and magnesium reduced
questions.exp: In uric acid nephropathy, S. K⁺, S. PO₄³⁻ and S. mg²⁺ all rise (↑) while serum calcium falls. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy (tumour lysis syndrome) · p801
questions.q: All but one of the following are features of uric acid nephropathy. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Uric acid nephropathy: oliguric AKI with ↑↑uric acid, ↑K⁺/PO₄/mg²⁺ and ↓Ca²⁺ — calcium falls, so hypercalcemia is not a feature. (Book p801)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy: treatment & prevention · p802
questions.q: Match the treatment of uric acid nephropathy — 1) Drug  2) Renal replacement … A) Dialysis  B) IV Rasburicase
questions.exp: Treatment of uric acid nephropathy: (1) IV rasburicase, (2) dialysis. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy: treatment & prevention · p802
questions.q: The IV drug used to treat uric acid nephropathy is:
questions.exp: Treatment: IV rasburicase along with dialysis; allopurinol appears under prevention (prophylaxis before chemotherapy). (Book p802)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy: treatment & prevention · p802
questions.q: The hydration advised before chemotherapy to prevent uric acid nephropathy is:
questions.exp: Prevention: adequate hydration (5–6 L/day) before chemotherapy, adequate alkalinization and allopurinol. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy: treatment & prevention · p802
questions.q: Match the three preventive measures for uric acid nephropathy — 1) Hydration (5–6 L/day)  2) Alkalinization  3) Allopurinol … A) All three are preventive measures before chemotherapy
opts: All three are preventive measures before chemotherapy
Only hydration prevents tumour lysis syndrome
All three are treatments given after AKI is established
questions.exp: Prevention of uric acid nephropathy: adequate hydration 5–6 L/day before chemotherapy, adequate alkalinization and allopurinol. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy: treatment & prevention · p802
questions.q: All but one of the following are preventive measures against uric acid nephropathy before chemotherapy. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Rasburicase is the IV treatment of established uric acid nephropathy; prevention consists of hydration 5–6 L/day, alkalinization and allopurinol. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Uric acid nephropathy: treatment & prevention · p802
questions.q: Allopurinol is listed under prevention of uric acid nephropathy rather than as the treatment of established disease.
opts: False — allopurinol is the treatment of established disease
False — allopurinol is used only for gout
questions.exp: Prevention before chemotherapy: hydration 5–6 L/day, alkalinization and allopurinol; established disease is treated with IV rasburicase and dialysis. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: Match the causes of rhabdomyolysis — 1) Electric shock  2) Seizures  3) Alcohol/cocaine/heroin  4) Statins/zidovudine … A) All are listed causes  B) None is a listed cause
opts: All four are listed causes of rhabdomyolysis
questions.exp: Causes of rhabdomyolysis: electric shock, seizures, alcohol/cocaine/heroin, statins/zidovudine, ↓K⁺/↓PO₄³⁻, glycogen storage disease type 5 (McArdle disease), hypothyroidism and polymyositis/dermatomyositis. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: Fill up: Glycogen storage disease type 5, also called ______ disease, is a listed cause of rhabdomyolysis.
questions.exp: Glycogen storage disease type 5 (McArdle disease) is a listed cause, along with hypothyroidism and polymyositis/dermatomyositis. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: All but one of the following are listed causes of rhabdomyolysis. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: The list includes ↓K⁺/↓PO₄³⁻ (hypokalemia/hypophosphatemia) as a cause; hyperkalemia is a consequence, not a cause. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: Match the pathophysiology of rhabdomyolysis — 1) Tubular effect  2) Vascular effect  3) Obstructive effect … A) Cast formation decreasing tubular flow  B) Direct toxicity of myoglobin in tubular cells  C) Hypovolemia and decreased renal perfusion
questions.exp: Rhabdomyolysis pathophysiology: PCT injury + vasoconstriction + tubular obstruction with uric acid; the diagram shows direct myoglobin toxicity, cast formation decreasing tubular flow, and hypovolemia with decreased renal perfusion — all leading to AKI. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: A young man with a crush injury has CK of 20,000 U/L and a creatinine that continues to rise beyond day 5. According to the note this suggests:
questions.exp: CPK assay: >1500 units, rising after 2–12 hrs, peaking in 1–3 days, falling in 3–5 days — if there is no fall, suspect compartment syndrome. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: The CPK level described as significant in rhabdomyolysis is:
questions.exp: CPK assay >1500 units rises after 2–12 hrs, peaks in 1–3 days and falls in 3–5 days. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: Match the rhabdomyolysis clinical features — 1) Muscles  2) Urine colour  3) Renal failure type  4) Urine sediment … A) Pigmented granular casts  B) Upper/lower-limb muscle cramps with high coloured urine  C) Non-oliguric AKI (pre-renal failure)  D) Proximal muscle swelling
questions.exp: Clinical features: upper/lower-limb muscle cramps with high coloured urine (2); proximal muscle swelling (4); non-oliguric AKI — pre-renal failure (3); urine shows pigmented granular casts (1). (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: All but one of the following investigations are raised in rhabdomyolysis. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Investigations in rhabdomyolysis: ↑S.K⁺, ↑S.PO₄³⁻, ↑S.mg²⁺ and ↑S. uric acid, with ↓S.Ca²⁺, acidosis (HAGMA) and FeNa <1. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: Match the urine findings in rhabdomyolysis — 1) Benzidine test  2) Urine microscopy … A) 3+ with no RBCs; pigmented granular brown casts; renal tubular epithelial cell casts  B) Positive for blood
questions.exp: Rhabdomyolysis urine: benzidine test 3+ but no RBCs; microscopy shows pigmented granular brown casts and renal tubular epithelial cell casts. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: Urine dipstick is positive for blood in a patient with rhabdomyolysis, but microscopy shows no RBCs. The explanation is:

The patient has a urinary tract infection
RBCs have all been lysed by alkaline urine
questions.exp: Benzidine test 3+ with no RBC on microscopy indicates myoglobinuria; casts seen are pigmented granular brown casts and renal tubular epithelial casts. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: The treatment of rhabdomyolysis consists of:
opts: Vigorous and intense hydration, alkalinization of urine and hemodialysis
Fluid restriction with diuretics and early high-dose corticosteroid therapy
Steroids with cyclophosphamide followed by a course of plasma exchange
IV rasburicase with allopurinol and hydration of 5–6 litres per day
questions.exp: Treatment of rhabdomyolysis: vigorous & intense hydration, alkalinization of urine and hemodialysis. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: The acidosis of rhabdomyolysis is a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA), unlike the NAGMA of ATN.
opts: False — rhabdomyolysis does not alter acid-base status
questions.exp: Investigations in rhabdomyolysis: acidosis (HAGMA) with FeNa <1; the ATN complication list specifies acidosis (NAGMA). (Book p802)

questions.sec: Rhabdomyolysis · p802
questions.q: All but one of the following belong to the rhabdomyolysis picture. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Rhabdomyolysis has FeNa <1 (pre-renal component predominant), non-oliguric AKI and pigmented granular brown casts. (Book p802)

questions.sec: Contrast-induced AKI · p803
questions.q: The incidence of contrast-induced AKI is reduced by using:
questions.exp: Contrast induced AKI: reduced incidence with low volume iso-osmolar contrast (iohexol/iopamidol). (Book p803)

questions.sec: Contrast-induced AKI · p803
questions.q: Fill up: The iso-osmolar contrast agents named for reducing contrast-induced AKI are ______ and iopamidol.

units.title: AKI definition, KDIGO staging and pre-renal causes
units.guide: AKI = abrupt fall in renal function over hours to days causing ECF volume expansion, uremia, hyperkalemia and acidosis. KDIGO stages by urine output and creatinine; newer markers NGAL, KIM-1, LFABP, IL-18. The CAUSES flowchart splits pre-renal (commonest hospital AKI) from renal (ATN, AIN) and post-renal; pre-renal causes run from volume depletion through reduced effective volume, low cardiac output, sepsis, renal vasoconstriction and compartment syndrome.

units.title: Pre-renal pathophysiology, ATN and AIN mechanisms
units.guide: Pre-renal failure is usually non-oliguric; oliguric pre-renal failure occurs only with renal vasoconstriction. Long-standing profound pre-renal failure causes ischemic ATN with tubuloglomerular feedback. ATN arises from ischemia and endogenous (hemoglobin, myoglobin, uric acid, light chains) or exogenous (drugs, contrast) toxins; AIN is a hypersensitivity reaction from drugs, infections (leptospirosis, scrub typhus) and infiltration (lymphoma, sarcoidosis).

units.title: Drug-induced AKI, pre-renal vs ATN table and FeNa
units.guide: Four drug columns: pre-renal (NSAIDs, calcium-elevating drugs, ACEi/ARB, calcineurin inhibitors), ATN (V, A, C, E, S mnemonics), intratubular obstruction/oliguric AKI (m, I, T, A, S) and AIN (PPIs, beta-lactams, rifampicin, allopurinol, anticonvulsants, NSAIDs, diuretics). Then the classic pre-renal vs ATN table line by line, the FeNa formula with normal 1-2%, the ATN-with-FeNa<1 exceptions, and the highest-yield unit still to come: AIN and drug nephropathy.

units.title: Acute interstitial nephritis and drug-induced nephropathy
units.guide: AIN is a T4-mediated hypersensitivity with reversible AKI: rash and eosinophilia, asymptomatic renal failure, no oedema or HTN, impaired RFT and mild proteinuria with occasional WBC casts, interstitial infiltrates with normal glomeruli on biopsy; treatment is stop the insult then steroids after a week. NSAID nephropathy (PG inhibition to RAAS) gives oliguria, FeNa <1 and hyperkalemia out of proportion; aminoglycosides bind megalin in the PCT brush border, accumulate in lysosomes and cause non-oliguric AKI 5-10 days later, prevented by single daily dosing.

units.title: ATN phases, sepsis pathology, features and investigations
units.guide: ATN has three phases (tubular injury, tubuloglomerular feedback with adenosine-mediated afferent vasoconstriction, recovery) with raised phosphorus/magnesium and low calcium; hypercalcemia and hypernatremia are not seen in AKI. Sepsis: pre-renal predominant over ATN, vasodilation with microthrombi and endothelial leak, PAMPs/DAMPs to inflammatory cascade to oxidative stress; causes and perfusion signs; investigations - IVC diameter 2-2.5 cm, lactate >1 and >4 mmol/L and the (obsolete) passive leg raising test.

units.title: Sepsis treatment ladder and uric acid nephropathy
units.guide: Sepsis-AKI treatment: crystalloid first, vasopressor second (norepinephrine > dopamine), dobutamine, cortisol; SAFE trial note; diuretics not used in prevention or treatment of AKI. Uric acid nephropathy (tumour lysis syndrome) follows chemotherapy of hematological malignancy with oliguric AKI, markedly raised uric acid, raised K/PO4/mg and low calcium, treated with IV rasburicase and dialysis, prevented by 5-6 L/day hydration, alkalinization and allopurinol.

units.title: Rhabdomyolysis
units.guide: Causes from electric shock and seizures to statins, hypokalemia/hypophosphatemia, McArdle disease, hypothyroidism and myositis; pathophysiology combines PCT injury, vasoconstriction and uric acid casts with myoglobin toxicity, cast obstruction and hypovolemia. Clinical features (cramps, swelling, non-oliguric AKI, pigmented granular casts), CPK kinetics with the compartment-syndrome caveat, HAGMA with FeNa <1, and treatment with vigorous hydration, alkalinization and hemodialysis.

units.title: Contrast-induced AKI and athero-embolic renal disease
units.guide: Contrast-induced AKI: reduced by low volume iso-osmolar contrast (iohexol/iopamidol), medullary hypoxia with tubular injury, creatinine rise at 24-48 hrs peaking at 3-5 days and normal in 7-10 days, no treatment required and prevention by hydration. Athero-embolic renal disease (cholesterol embolism) after endovascular intervention in extensive aortic atherosclerosis, with subacute renal failure over weeks, blue toe, livedo reticularis, Hollenhorst plaque, poor prognosis, hypocomplementemia, eosinophiluria with Hansel's stain, raised amylase, skin (never kidney) biopsy showing birefringent biconvex cholesterol crystals and ACE inhibitor avoidance.

units.guide: CRS 1-5 table: acute cardiorenal, chronic cardiorenal, acute renocardiac, chronic renocardiac and secondary, each with its definition. The closing note: snake bite, placental abruption and pancreatitis cause acute cortical necrosis (urine output failing to recover) that can progress to CKD.
